content.title: About
content.content: Apple cake or cupcake is a baked good that incorporates fresh or baked apples into the batter or frosting. It offers a delicate apple aroma, a mildly sweet‑tart flavor, and a moist, tender crumb. A cake is typically taller and layered, while a cupcake is a single‑serve, compact version.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Apple cupcakes are especially popular in the autumn harvest season when apples are abundant.
The classic American "Apple Crumble" inspired many modern apple cake recipes.
Adding cinnamon and nutmeg enhances the apple scent and gives the pastry a warm spice note.
Apple‑based baked goods can be made gluten‑free (using alternative flours) or vegan (replacing eggs and dairy).
A 19th‑century apple cake recipe called for honey instead of refined sugar.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Apples provide both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting healthy digestion.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C in apples acts as an antioxidant that helps protect cells.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids and polyphenols in apples combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Fiber and potassium help maintain normal cholesterol levels and blood pressure.

items.title: Moderate natural sugar
items.content: Compared with pure sweets, apple cake derives sweetness from fruit sugars, making it less sugary.

items.title: Wheat or egg allergy
items.content: Traditional recipes contain wheat flour and eggs, which can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Some versions use large amounts of sugar or syrups, increasing calorie load.

items.title: Gluten content
items.content: People with celiac disease should use gluten‑free flour alternatives.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Apples can raise acidity, which may be problematic for those with gastritis.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the cake or cupcake as a dessert with tea or coffee, cut into portions, and optionally top with whipped cream, ice cream, or caramel sauce. Cool it before serving for a firmer texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days or refrigerate for up to 5 days. For longer storage, freeze in freezer‑safe bags for up to 2 months. Allow to reach room temperature before eating.

chicken-thigh-ns-as-to-cooking-method-sk.title: Chicken thigh, skin-on, cooking method – frying, skin eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken thigh is the dark meat located on the upper part of the bird’s leg. It is juicier and more flavorful than breast meat due to a higher fat content. When prepared with the skin left on, the meat retains more flavor, and the crispy skin adds texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken thighs are a staple in many world cuisines, from fried chicken to stews.
The fat in the skin contains monounsaturated fatty acids that can be beneficial in moderation.
During frying, the skin becomes crisp while the meat underneath stays moist.
Chicken provides a good source of protein, B‑vitamins, and minerals such as phosphorus and selenium.
In some cultures, thighs are considered a more “festive” cut than breast meat.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Chicken thigh supplies complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It is rich in niacin (B3), vitamin B6 and B12, which support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Phosphorus and selenium in the meat contribute to bone health and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Energy‑dense skin
items.content: The edible skin adds extra calories and helps promote satiety when eaten in reasonable amounts.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: Chicken is generally easy on the stomach, making it suitable for most age groups.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Thighs with skin contain more fat, so portion control is advisable for those watching calorie intake.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Raw chicken can harbor salmonella; cook to an internal temperature of 75 °C (165 °F) to ensure safety.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to chicken proteins.

items.title: Hormones and antibiotics
items.content: Choose certified or responsibly raised birds to minimize exposure to residues.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Thighs can be fried, baked, braised, or grilled. For frying, sear the skin until golden, then finish cooking the meat. They pair well with herbs, spices, soy sauce, and lemon. Use them in salads, soups, stews, or serve as a main dish.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh chicken thighs refrigerated at 0‑4 °C for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze in airtight packaging at –18 °C for up to 6 months. Thaw frozen thighs in the refrigerator, not at room temperature, before cooking.

content.title: About
content.content: Cookie, butter and sugar are basic ingredients often used together in baking and confectionery. Cookie can be a finished product or a base for desserts. Butter (usually dairy) adds flavor, aroma and structure, while sugar provides sweetness and promotes caramelization.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first cookies appeared in Persia in the 9th century and were called “khurmah”.
Butter has been produced by churning cream since ancient times; large‑scale production in Europe began in the 17th century.
White sugar from sugarcane was a luxury in Europe until the 19th century when modern refining methods emerged.
The combination of cookie, butter and sugar is used in classic recipes such as shortbread and gingerbread.
Granulated sugar influences cookie texture, making it crisper.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: The mix of carbohydrates (sugar) and fats (butter) provides a quick source of energy, useful during intense physical activity.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Butter contains vitamins A, D, E and K, as well as fatty acids important for skin and vision health.

items.title: Mood enhancement
items.content: Sugar stimulates serotonin production, which can temporarily improve mood.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Excessive sugar intake is linked to increased risk of cavities, obesity and metabolic disorders.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Butter is rich in saturated fats, which can raise cholesterol levels when consumed in excess.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to lactose or milk proteins present in butter.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cookies can be enjoyed as a snack or used in desserts (tarts, cheesecakes). Butter is melted and incorporated into dough to improve texture. Sugar is used as granules, powder or syrup to control sweetness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cookies in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Butter is best kept refrigerated in a tightly sealed package to prevent oxidation. Sugar should be kept dry, protected from moisture, in a sealed container.

content.title: About
content.content: Dry roasted unsalted peanuts are whole peanuts that have been heat‑treated at a low temperature, preserving their natural flavor while giving them a crunchy texture. No salt is added, making them suitable for low‑sodium diets.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Peanuts are legumes, not true nuts.
Dry roasting retains more nutrients than oil roasting.
Peanuts are a staple in many Asian cuisines, appearing in sauces, salads, and snacks.
Dry roasted peanuts have a lower fat content than oil‑roasted peanuts.
Peanuts provide a plant‑based source of protein for vegetarians.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Peanuts contain about 25 % protein, supporting muscle maintenance and satiety.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: They are rich in monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids, beneficial for heart health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Peanuts supply niacin, thiamine, and folate, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: They provide magnesium, phosphorus, iron, and zinc, supporting muscles, bones, and immunity.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Compounds such as resveratrol and phenolics help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Peanuts can trigger severe allergic reactions in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Calorie dense
items.content: Even dry roasted, peanuts are calorie‑rich, so portion control is advised.

items.title: Aflatoxin risk
items.content: Improper storage can lead to aflatoxin formation, a toxin harmful to the liver.

items.title: Choking hazard for children
items.content: Whole dry roasted peanuts may pose a choking risk for young children.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Dry roasted unsalted peanuts make a convenient snack, can be tossed into salads, oatmeal, yogurt, or used in baking and sauces. A quick toss in a hot pan can enhance their aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For long‑term storage, refrigerate or freeze to prevent fat oxidation. Discard if the peanuts become rancid or develop an off‑smell.

rice-brown-with-gravy-no-added-fat.title: Brown Rice with Gravy, No Added Fat

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice is a whole‑grain product obtained from the whole grain after removing only the outer hull. In this version the rice is served with a lean gravy prepared without added oil or fat, making the dish low‑calorie and suitable for diet plans.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice retains the bran and germ, so it contains more fiber, vitamins, and minerals than white rice.
Fat‑free gravy is usually made from vegetable broth, tomatoes, and spices.
Brown rice has a lower glycemic index than white rice, helping to stabilize blood sugar levels.
Rice is traditionally used in Asian cuisines but is now popular worldwide in health‑focused diets.
When stored properly, whole brown rice can stay fresh for up to 6 months.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps maintain gut health.

items.title: Source of magnesium and selenium
items.content: Magnesium aids muscle and nerve function, while selenium provides antioxidant protection.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The absence of added fat makes the dish suitable for calorie‑restricted diets.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B3, and B6 support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Supports blood sugar control
items.content: A low glycemic index helps avoid rapid spikes in blood glucose after meals.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Brown rice contains phytic acid, which can reduce the absorption of certain minerals if consumed in excess.

items.title: Arsenic
items.content: Like other whole grains, brown rice may contain trace amounts of arsenic; a varied diet is recommended.

items.title: Rice allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to rice.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the rice as a side dish with vegetables, fish, or lean meat. Prepare the gravy from tomato puree, onion, garlic, and herbs, thickening it without oil. Add fresh herbs or a squeeze of lemon for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep dry brown rice in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked rice and gravy should be refrigerated and consumed within 3‑4 days.
